title: Your First Upwork Client With Zero Reviews: A Practical Plan
excerpt: How to land your first Upwork client with zero reviews: picking winnable jobs, pricing your first contract, and proposals that build trust fast.

content:
Landing your first Upwork client is the one step nobody gets to skip, and it's where most people get stuck. You have a profile, maybe a solid portfolio, a handful of Connects, and a big empty space where reviews, Job Success Score and earnings history should be. I've been there. I had years of professional engineering experience before I started taking Upwork seriously in September 2024, and none of it showed up in the places a client actually looks. This is the practical plan I'd follow if I were starting from zero reviews again today.

Why Your First Upwork Client Is the Hardest One

Every hire on Upwork is a risk decision. The client is about to hand money and a deadline to a stranger on the other side of the world. Reviews, hire counts and badges exist to reduce that risk. When you have none of them, the client isn't judging your skill yet. They're judging how risky you feel.

That reframe changed how I approached everything. My job wasn't to prove I was the best developer on the platform. It was to make hiring me feel like a safe, low-regret decision. Experience at companies, side projects and real apps all count, but only if you translate them into signals a nervous client can see in a few seconds.

The other thing worth knowing: your first job doesn't have to be tiny. My first real project was a MERN stack platform for a Jiu Jitsu business, and the first payment was around $3,000. I'm not saying that's typical or that you should expect it. I'm saying the idea that you must start with a $20 task is a myth. What matters is that the job fits your proven skills closely enough that the client believes you can deliver.

Reality check

My progress wasn't a straight line. Year one averaged roughly $1K+ per month, and my real breakthrough didn't come until January 2025. Nobody can promise you a timeline, and anyone who does is selling something. Treat the first client as a project you work on deliberately, not a lottery ticket.

Choosing Jobs You Can Actually Win

Most beginners lose before they write a word, because they apply to the wrong jobs. Spraying Connects across every posting that mentions your stack burns money and confidence. With zero reviews, you need to be ruthless about where you compete.

Signals worth chasing

  • Posted recently with few proposals. Being early matters more than people admit. A thoughtful proposal in the first hour gets read; proposal number 48 often doesn't.
  • Payment method verified. This is a basic sign the client is serious.
  • A specific, well-described problem. Clear scope means you can show you understood it, which is your biggest advantage over generic applicants.
  • An exact match with your strongest skill. If you've shipped Android apps in Kotlin for years, a Kotlin bug-fix or feature job is where your lack of reviews matters least.
  • Clients who've hired before but still reply to new freelancers. Look at their history and how they talk about past freelancers in feedback.

Signals to skip

  • Huge scope with a tiny budget, like a full marketplace app for a few hundred dollars.
  • Vague one-line descriptions where you'd be guessing what they want.
  • Requests to communicate or pay outside the platform.
  • Jobs that require work samples done for free as a test.

I'd rather send five sharp proposals a day to jobs I can genuinely win than twenty forgettable ones. Narrowing your focus also helps your profile, because a specialist is easier to trust than a generalist with no track record.

How to Price Your First Contract

Freelance pricing is where new freelancers panic and race to the bottom. I understand the instinct, but a suspiciously low rate doesn't reduce risk in the client's eyes. It often increases it. Serious clients wonder why a skilled person is charging so little, and the clients attracted by rock-bottom prices tend to be the hardest to work with.

Here's how I think about it:

  1. Know your target rate, the one you'd charge once you have a few reviews.
  2. Start modestly below it for your first contract or two, not at a fraction of it. The discount buys trust, not desperation.
  3. Reduce risk with structure, not just price. Offer a small, clearly defined first milestone. The client gets to test you with limited exposure, and you get paid for real work.
  4. Raise your rate as soon as reviews land. Your intro pricing is temporary, and you should treat it that way from day one.

A small fixed-price first milestone is one of the most effective trust bridges I know. Something like: set up the project, fix the most urgent bug, or deliver one complete screen with tests. I've written separately about choosing between hourly and fixed price, but for a first contract, a tightly scoped milestone usually feels safest to the client.

Don't do this

Don't work for free, don't accept payment outside Upwork, and don't start work before a contract and funded milestone are in place. Zero reviews is a temporary problem. Losing payment protection or getting your account flagged is a much bigger one.

Writing Proposals When You Have No Reviews

Your proposal has to do the work your review history can't. That means it needs to prove three things fast: you understood the problem, you've solved something like it before, and working with you will be easy.

Lead with their problem, not your biography

The first two lines show up in the client's preview. If they start with your name, your years of experience or a greeting, you've wasted the most valuable space you have. Start by restating their problem in sharper terms than they did, then hint at how you'd approach it.

Your app is losing scroll position and form state when users switch away and come back. That usually points to state not surviving process death. I've fixed this pattern in production Kotlin apps and can walk you through how I'd approach it in your codebase.

Replace reviews with proof

Since you can't point to Upwork feedback, point to things a client can verify:

  • Live apps or websites you built, with your exact role described honestly.
  • A GitHub repository that shows clean, relevant code.
  • A short case study: the problem, what you did, and the outcome.
  • A brief screen recording walking through a similar project.

One strong, relevant example beats a list of ten loosely related ones.

Address being new, briefly and confidently

You don't need to hide that you're new on Upwork, and you shouldn't apologize for it either. One sentence is enough: you're new to the platform, not new to the work, and here's the proof. Then pair it with that low-risk first milestone so the client has an easy way to say yes.

End with one sharp question

A specific question about their project, like which Android versions they support or whether they have an existing API, invites a reply and shows you're already thinking about the work. Replies turn into interviews, and interviews are where you'll win your first job.

Turning Your First Upwork Client Into Momentum

Winning your first Upwork client is the start, not the finish. The way you handle that first contract shapes your next several jobs, because your first review carries a lot of weight on an empty profile.

Overdeliver on communication, not on scope. New freelancers often try to impress by doing extra unrequested work. That leads to scope creep and blurred expectations. What clients remember is clarity: regular updates, early warnings about blockers, and no guessing about where things stand. In my client work, consistent communication has mattered as much as the code itself, especially with US clients who are often several time zones away.

Make the end of the contract clean. Deliver what was agreed, summarize what you did, note anything they should know going forward, and then ask for feedback. Don't beg for five stars. A simple message saying you'd appreciate honest feedback on the contract is professional and works well.

Look for the next piece of work. The easiest second job is often from your first client. If you noticed other issues in their codebase, mention them as suggestions, not a sales pitch. Repeat work from a happy client is one of the strongest signals you can build early.

Update your profile immediately. Add the project to your portfolio, tighten your headline around what you just delivered, and adjust your rate if it makes sense.

Momentum compounds slowly and then quickly. For me, it took months of steady, unglamorous work before things clicked. Since then I've reached Top Rated Plus and earned $70K+ across roughly 18 jobs in about a year and a half, with around 70% of my clients in the US. I share that not as a promise of what you'll earn, but to show that the first client really is the hardest door, and the rest of the path is built on it. If you want to talk through this stuff with others on the same road, that's exactly what the Build With Aamir WhatsApp community is for.

Key Takeaways

  • With zero reviews, clients judge your risk before your skill, so your job is to make hiring you feel safe.
  • Apply only to recent, specific, verified jobs that closely match your strongest proven skills.
  • Price modestly below your target rate rather than at rock bottom, and use a small paid first milestone to reduce client risk.
  • Write proposals that lead with the client's problem, replace missing reviews with verifiable proof, and end with one specific question.
  • Treat your first contract as a foundation: communicate clearly, finish cleanly, ask for feedback, and update your profile right away.
